draft.title: CRISPR-Cas9
card: Bacteria use CRISPR as a defence against viruses. They store short pieces of viral DNA and use them to recognise and cut that virus if it returns.
a short RNA made to match the target DNA sequence. It pairs with the target and leads Cas9 to the chosen place.
an enzyme that cuts both strands of DNA at the place the guide RNA has found.
Scientists change the guide RNA to aim Cas9 at a chosen gene. The cell then repairs the cut, which can disable the gene or let a new sequence be added.
draft.remember: Guide RNA finds the place. Cas9 makes the cut.

a.q: In CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, what is the job of the guide RNA?
opts: It leads Cas9 to the matching target DNA sequence
It cuts both strands of DNA at the target
It repairs the DNA after the cut is made
It copies the target gene into new cells
a.why: The guide RNA has a sequence that pairs with the target DNA, so it leads Cas9 to the right place. Cas9 is the enzyme that cuts, so the guide RNA does not do the cutting.
a.clue: Which part matches the target sequence?

b.q: A team wants Cas9 to cut a different gene in a mouse cell, using the same Cas9 enzyme. What must they change?
opts: The sequence of the guide RNA
The type of enzyme that cuts the DNA
The bacterial virus that supplies Cas9
The number of DNA strands the cut goes through
b.why: The guide RNA decides where Cas9 cuts, so a new target needs a new guide RNA that matches it. Cas9 can stay the same because it cuts wherever it is led.
b.clue: Which part decides the place of the cut?

a.best: It leads Cas9 to the matching target DNA sequence

b.best: The sequence of the guide RNA
